catalog_quote: Hiligaynon has twenty-five significant sounds plus accent. ... Accented words have one primary stress. Some words have no stress of their own but rather "lean" on words which do. Stressless words are referred to as clitics or particles. A cluster of a stressed word together with one or more particles is a stress group. ... 1.2. Accent and Intonation. The term accent here refers to the emphasizing of a syllable in a word by means of loudness, vowel length, pitch, or a combination of these. Some words may have more than one accented syllable. All words except the grammatical particles have one primary accented syllable and if more than two syllables usually a secondary accent on one of the other syllables. Intonation refers to the sequence of pitch levels through a sentence. No data are yet available on the intonation patterns of Hiligaynon. Primary accent is lexically significant as can …

audit.recode_to: kind stays 'lexical'. Optional refinement from Zorc 1977 sec. 3.1.3/10.2.1 and Zorc 2001 p. 301: accent window = final two syllables (penult or ultima); words with a closed penult (CVC.CV(C)) take penult accent predictably, so the lexical contrast is confined to open-penult words; accented open penult realised as vowel length. This would replace the prule sentence 'No positional or weight-based rule is stated' and could populate the edge/weight fields.
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: every clause of the deciding quotation is verbatim in the held djvu text of Wolfenden 1971 at the stated places (sec. 1 p. 10; sec. 1.2 pp. 24-25) and the held page image of printed p. 25 shows the minimal pairs with accents. (2) Deciding source is a 238-pp linguist's reference grammar (1971), the standard description of the language; Glottolog lists no phonology monograph, no JIPA Illustration exists (checked), and Crossref shows no stress/prosody study. The two specialist sources by Zorc (1977 comparative Bisayan monograph, held; 2001 encyclopedia sketch, fetched sources now) and Motus 1971 (fetched sources now) all independently state that accent is lexically contrastive, so the LEXICAL coding is secure. (3) Zorc adds two facts Wolfenden does not state: accent is limited to the last two syllables, and closed-penult words are predictably penult-accented; these refine, not contradict

sources.citation: Motus, Cecile L. 1971. Hiligaynon Lessons. PALI Language Texts: Philippines. Honolulu: University of Hawaii Press. xxiii+430 pp. (archive.org item HiligaynonLessons, djvu text layer)
sources.quote: 'Stress is important in Hiligaynon in that it makes for a difference in meaning in some instances ... One syllable is pronounced louder than the other or others. This prominence is called stress. Example: punu' means 'tree trunk, leader, etc.' while punu' [other accent] means 'full to capacity'.' Drill lists accent pairs laba/laba', punu'/punu', bulag/bulag, pilak/pilak. (Same statement in Motus 1971 Hiligaynon Dictionary intro sec. III, fetched sources as : 'Stress is phonemic in Hiligaynon'.)

sources.quote: 'Word accent is very important in distinguishing forms in Hiligaynon. Roots generally have accent on either the second last or final syllable, as in: ámo 'master' (Sp.) vs. amó 'the same, thus', áyaw ... vs. ayáw ..., bála vs. balá, báti vs. batí, bílin vs. bilín, dúlot vs. dulút, súbong vs. subóng, and útud vs. utúd. If the accent falls on the second last syllable (penult) and that syllable is not closed by a consonant ... the vowel is pronounced long ... sources.note: Most recent specialist statement: accent falls on penult or final (two-syllable window), eight minimal pairs, phonetic realisation (length on open penult, stress+pitch on final); a second independent citation for the LEXICAL coding.

sources.citation: Zorc, R. David Paul. 1977. The Bisayan Dialects of the Philippines: Subgrouping and Reconstruction. Pacific Linguistics C-44. Canberra: ANU. 352 pp. (open PDF from zorc.net; Hiligaynon = 'Hil', one of the 36 Bs dialects surveyed from fieldwork)
sources.quote: 3.1.3: 'The accentual systems of all other Bs dialects [i.e. all but Kuy and Tsg] have phonetic details involving both vowel length and stress. The vowel in an accented open penult is long ... In all dialects studied (except Kuy) stems or derivatives with a closed penult [CVC.CV(C)] are accented on the penult (see 10.2.1.).' 10.2.1: 'It is an innovation of importance for subgrouping that all Bs dialects have penultimate rather than ultimate stress on inherited words with a closed penult ... inherited forms with a closed penult show no contrasts of stress, i.e., the stress is predictable from t
sources.locator: sec. 3.1.3 'Accent', printed pp. 50-51 = PDF pp. 74-75; sec. 10.2.1, printed p. 243 = PDF p. 267
sources.note: Specialist comparative phonology covering Hiligaynon from fieldwork; states the sub-regularity our prule says is absent (closed penult -> penult accent, contrast only with open penult) and that accented open penults are long. Held on file but not cited in the record.
